summary: This Standards Track document defines an RDAP extension so Time-to-Live values for relevant DNS record types can be included in RDAP responses.

eli5.summary: When looking up a website's registration card, you can also see how long its address sticks around.

questions: how do i get dns ttl from rdap
what is the ttl0 rdap extension
subtitle: An RDAP extension that lets registries show the configured DNS TTL values for a domain or nameserver.

tldr.problem: RDAP can already report a domain's NS, DS, A and AAAA data, but not the Time-to-Live values of those RRsets, which makes out-of-band debugging of troublesome domains harder.
tldr.mechanism: Servers MAY add a ttl0_data object to domain and nameserver objects. Its values member maps DNS record type mnemonics to TTL numbers, and the response lists ttl0 in rdapConformance.
tldr.outcome: Operators and clients can see the TTLs provisioned in the registry database, not the remaining TTL seen in live DNS queries.

today: RFC 10037 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2026, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It pairs with the EPP mapping in RFC 9803.

sections.title: Why RDAP Needs TTL Values
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) gives access to information about domain names, autonomous system numbers and IP addresses. RFC 9083 lets servers describe the content of the NS, DS, A and AAAA RRsets published in the DNS for a registry object, but it has no way to include the Time-to-Live (TTL) of those RRsets.

Adding the TTLs, alongside nameservers, glue IP addresses and Delegation Signer (DS) records, allows out-of-band debugging of the DNS configuration of troublesome domain names. As in RFC 2181, TTLs apply to RRsets rather than to individual records.
sections.eli5: The registration card already says who answers questions about a website. It did not say how long people may remember the answer. Now it can.

sections.title: The ttl0_data Member
sections.content:
Servers that support the extension MAY include a ttl0_data member in any domain or nameserver object in an RDAP response. Clients that do not implement the extension SHOULD ignore it.

The member is an object with two parts: a values member that maps DNS record type mnemonics to TTL values, and an OPTIONAL remarks member, which is an array of RDAP remarks.

TTL values MUST be JSON numbers with no fractional component and no exponent notation. The values MUST reflect the TTLs as provisioned in the registry database, not the remaining TTL of records seen in live DNS queries.
sections.eli5: It is a little box on the card with two parts: a list saying "this kind of record, this many seconds", and an optional note from the registry.

sections.title: Record Types and TTL Ranges
sections.content:
The member names in values are DNS record type mnemonics. They MUST be in all capitals and MUST be registered with IANA as resource record types.

A TTL MUST be an unsigned integer from 0 to 2147483647, as RFC 2181 defines. A domain example in the RFC carries NS and DS values, and a nameserver example carries A and AAAA values.
sections.eli5: Record names are written in capital letters, and the number of seconds cannot be negative or bigger than the largest allowed number.

sections.title: Declaring Conformance
sections.content: Servers returning responses with TTL values MUST include the string ttl0 in the rdapConformance array. That is how a client knows the extension is in use. IANA has registered ttl0 in the RDAP Extensions registry, with registry operator Any.
sections.eli5: A response with TTLs must wave a small flag named ttl0 so the reader knows the extra box is there.

sections.title: Notes for Servers and Clients
sections.content:
Servers. The extension complements the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) and the EPP mapping for DNS TTL values in RFC 9803, but registry operators do not need to implement that EPP extension to implement this one.

Clients. Many RDAP clients use frameworks that automatically "hydrate" objects from JSON, so they should explicitly carve out the values member of ttl0_data. Because the record types may change over time, clients that implement the extension MUST accept values for all valid DNS record types and SHOULD periodically update their list from the IANA registry to avoid discarding a recently added type.
sections.eli5: Servers do not need the matching registration-system feature first. Readers should be ready for new kinds of records to show up, rather than throwing away ones they have not seen before.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security services for the extension are those described in RFC 7481. The document concerns only how configured TTL values for domain and host objects are represented. How a registry determines, assigns or modifies those values is out of scope, and the RFC points readers to Section 6 of RFC 9803 for that discussion.
sections.eli5: This note only describes how to show the numbers. It does not say who may change them, which is covered elsewhere.
